spans.assertion: the analysis used a dataset of 146,028 player-referee dyads from elite European soccer leagues (2012-2013 season) to test whether referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players
the primary analysis compared 9,481 dyads involving dark-skinned players (skin tone ≥0.75) to 84,050 dyads involving light-skinned players (skin tone ≤0.25)

the hypothesis that referees favor giving red cards to dark-skinned players was not supported at the conventional α=0.05 level; because the CI included zero and p exceeded 0.05, the evidence is characterized as inconclusive rather than as showing no effect
the adjusted risk difference was found to be 0.185 percentage points (95% CI -0.071 to 0.450, p=0.144)
the adjusted red card rate was 1.40% for dark-skinned players versus 1.21% for light-skinned players
the secondary analysis found an adjusted odds ratio of 1.160 (95% CI 0.921-1.461, p=0.208, using player-clustered standard errors), not statistically significant
sensitivity analyses found substantial heterogeneity by league country: a strong positive effect in Germany (OR=2.53, p<0.001) versus null or negative effects in France and Spain
using continuous skin tone over the full sample yielded a statistically significant result (OR=1.27 per unit increase, p=0.039), suggesting the dichotomization may have reduced power
the primary estimand results were: risk difference=0.185 percentage points, 95% CI (-0.071, 0.450), two-sided p=0.144, obtained via bootstrap with 999 successful iterations

after adjusting for number of games, player position, and league country, the model estimated dark-skinned players have a 0.185 percentage point higher probability of a red card, with a 95% CI (-0.071 to +0.450) that includes zero, so the null of no difference could not be rejected at α=0.05
predicted red card rates were 1.211% for light-skinned players and 1.396% for dark-skinned players
the secondary estimand results were: odds ratio=1.160, 95% CI (0.921, 1.461), p=0.208, using player-clustered standard errors
the odds of a red card for dark-skinned players were 1.16 times that of light-skinned players after covariate adjustment, with a CI including 1.0, consistent with the primary analysis

the model without clustered standard errors gave an identical odds ratio (1.160) but a different CI (0.956-1.407) and p-value (0.132); player-clustering was used because it yields more conservative inference
the unit of analysis was defined as the player-referee dyad, aggregating all encounters between one player and one referee into a single observation
the final analytic sample comprised 93,531 dyads: 84,050 involving light-skinned players (1,017 red cards) and 9,481 involving dark-skinned players (133 red cards)
the sample included 1,141 unique players and 2,753 unique referees
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator of whether the dyad resulted in any red card, rather than counting the number of cards
the base rate was found to be 1.23% of dyads involving at least one red card
skin tone was measured by two independent raters, blind to the research question, who rated each player's photo on a 5-point scale from 0 (very light) to 1 (very dark)
inter-rater correlation was found to be 0.923
a composite skin tone score was computed as the average of the two raters' scores
light skin was defined as an average rating of ≤0.25
dark skin was defined as an average rating of ≥0.75
dyads in the medium skin-tone category (0.25 < average < 0.75), 24,094 of them, were excluded from the primary analysis
the dichotomization of skin tone was chosen because it creates clearly distinguishable comparison groups and reduces measurement error, at the cost of statistical power
the logistic regression model was adjusted for three covariates: number of games, player position, and league country
number of games in the dyad was included as a continuous covariate, ranging from 1-47 with a mean of 3.1
games was treated as a critical exposure-opportunity variable, on the reasoning that more games means more opportunity for red cards
games was found to be a strong predictor of red cards, OR=1.14 per additional game, p<0.001
player position was included as a categorical covariate with 12 levels, intended to control for different playing styles and aggression levels
the reference category for position was set to Attacking Midfielder
center backs were found to have the highest red card risk (OR=2.84, p<0.001)
league country was included as a categorical covariate (England, France, Germany, Spain), intended to control for different refereeing cultures and league-level factors
the reference category for league country was set to England
France and Spain were found to have higher red card rates than England (both p<0.001)

dark-skinned players were found to be disproportionately represented in England (41%) and France (27%) versus Germany (19%) and Spain (13%), while light-skinned players were more evenly distributed; this imbalance was controlled for in the model
21,407 dyads (14.7% of the original sample) were excluded due to missing skin tone ratings from unavailable photos
players excluded for missing skin tone ratings were found not to be systematically different in red card rates
6,996 dyads (5.6%) with complete skin tone data were excluded due to missing position data
the red card rate among dyads with missing position was found to be 1.34%, similar to the overall rate
24,094 dyads in the medium skin-tone category were excluded by design from the primary analysis to create clear comparison groups
the total exclusion rate from the original dataset was found to be 36%
no transformations were applied to continuous variables
skin tone was dichotomized, as described in the exposure definition
the outcome was coded as binary (any red card versus none)
the primary inference approach used a non-parametric bootstrap with 999 successful iterations to obtain the confidence interval and p-value for the adjusted risk difference
the bootstrap approach was chosen because it makes minimal distributional assumptions, accounts for model estimation uncertainty, and yields valid inference under general conditions
a secondary inference approach used player-clustered standard errors for the logistic regression model
player-clustering was chosen to address within-player correlation (mean 82 dyads per player) and to give a conservative adjustment for multiple observations per player
two-way clustering by both player and referee was considered but not implemented, because it was not feasible with the available software
sensitivity to referee-level clustering is believed to be minimal, since 84% of referees gave zero red cards in the sample
the model was specified as a logistic regression: logit(P(red card)) = β0 + β1(dark_skin) + β2(games) + β3(position) + β4(league_country)
the risk difference was calculated by predicting P(red card) for each dyad under two counterfactual scenarios: the player being dark-skinned versus light-skinned
these counterfactual predictions were averaged across all dyads
the risk difference was computed as the mean predicted probability under the dark-skinned scenario minus the mean under the light-skinned scenario
this marginal-effects approach is described as yielding the average treatment effect on the probability scale
convergence was achieved in all bootstrap iterations (999 of 1000 successful)
the model's pseudo R² was found to be 0.076, described as a modest fit expected for a rare binary outcome
no evidence of separation or multicollinearity was found

the hypothesis was not supported: although the point estimate suggests a small positive association (0.185 percentage points, or a 16% relative increase), the 95% CI includes zero and p=0.144 exceeds α=0.05, so the null of no difference could not be rejected after adjustment

the estimated overall effect is described (in truncated/garbled text) as attributable almost entirely to Germany, with no evidence of bias found in other countries, raising questions about what is unique to the German context
an interaction between skin tone and number of games was tested, with a coefficient of 0.002 (p=0.90)
the effect of skin tone was found not to vary by exposure opportunity (number of games)

despite high inter-rater reliability (r=0.92), the 5-point skin tone scale is said to collapse complex phenotypic variation and may introduce misclassification bias, particularly for players near category boundaries
photo-based ratings may differ from how referees actually perceive players live on the field, given differences in dynamics, distance, and lighting
excluding the medium skin-tone category (stated here as 19% of the sample) reduces statistical power and may miss non-linear effects

excluding the 14.7% of dyads with missing photos could bias results if photo availability is related to both skin tone and red card risk, e.g. if less prominent players are both less likely to have a photo and less likely to receive a red card
exploratory checks on the 5.6% of dyads dropped for missing position suggested this exclusion is unlikely to cause major bias
the sample, restricted to players with enough career longevity in elite leagues to encounter multiple referees, may reflect survivorship bias by potentially selecting for less aggressive players
the model controlled for games played, position, and league country

player aggression or playing style was not controlled for; position is described as only a crude proxy, and if aggression correlates with skin tone (e.g. via positional preferences) it could confound the estimated effect
team quality and tactics were not controlled for; if dark-skinned players are concentrated on teams of different quality, this could bias results
referee-level characteristics (implicit/explicit bias) were not controlled for; country-level referee data were available but not used, due to modeling complexity
reputation effects — players with prior red cards possibly being treated differently by referees — were not accounted for
only 1.2% of dyads involved a red card, a rare outcome that was found to limit statistical power
the exposure was unbalanced: 90% of dyads were light-skinned and 10% dark-skinned
multiple sensitivity analyses were conducted, using continuous skin tone, different categorizations, and stratifications
the sensitivity analyses were pre-specified in the analysis plan
the Germany finding (p<0.001) was found to remain robust even after a Bonferroni correction for 4 countries (threshold p<0.0125)
the sample includes only 4 European countries
the data are from the 2012-2013 season, described as over a decade old
the sample is restricted to elite professional leagues only, and results may not extend to lower levels or other regions
the sample includes male players only
the independence-of-raters assumption is said to be met by design, since raters worked independently and were blind to the hypothesis
the covariate-measurement assumption is said to be met, since games, position, and league are objectively measured
the logistic model's functional form is said to appear reasonable, given the rare binary outcome and no evidence of misspecification
bootstrap validity is said to be supported by the large sample size (>90,000)
the missing-completely-at-random assumption is flagged as uncertain, since missing photos may be related to player prominence or skill
the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption is described as a strong assumption likely violated to some degree
the positivity assumption is potentially violated, since very few dark-skinned players occupy some positions (e.g. only 0.8% of attacking midfielders)
the homogeneity-of-effect assumption is violated, given strong evidence of heterogeneity by league

the unadjusted risk difference (0.193 percentage points) was found to be very similar to the adjusted estimate (0.185), suggesting confounders had minimal impact and increasing confidence that the adjusted estimate is not an artifact of model specification

additional player-level statistics were found: a mean of 1.03 red cards per player across career, 622 players (55%) receiving at least one red card, and a highly skewed distribution with a maximum of 13

even at the upper bound of the CI (0.45pp), the absolute effect is said to remain small, translating to roughly 5-6 additional red cards for dark-skinned players per season across all four leagues combined, though cumulative career effects could be more substantial

the analysis code is provided in final_analysis.py, reproducible from the source data file ./data/soccer/soccer.csv, and was run in Python 3.11 using pandas 2.0+, statsmodels 0.14+, numpy, scipy, and matplotlib

the analysis concludes there was insufficient evidence to support the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players after adjusting for key confounders, and the evidence should be characterized as inconclusive rather than as contradicting the hypothesis

sensitivity analyses revealed strong heterogeneity by country — a large, significant effect in Germany but null or negative effects elsewhere — leading to the conclusion that any bias, if present, is context-specific rather than universal

the small absolute effect size, even at the upper CI bound, suggests that if bias exists it is subtle rather than pervasive, though the high-stakes nature of red-card decisions is said to warrant continued attention and monitoring

spans.note: generic caveats about the observational design, speculative causal mechanisms, and clustering/power effects, without naming a specific analytic action or number
forward-looking recommendations for future research, not actions taken or findings of this analysis
